messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arun Patel is a 79-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment only after months of pressure from his adult daughter, who had grown worried about how narrowed and strained his life had become. Divorced for many years, he lives alone and still works part-time in a warehouse, a routine he has kept with a kind of stern determination. He speaks in a spare, disciplined way, as if he has spent decades training himself to say no more than necessary. When he first describes his history, the central fact is his combat experience as a young man, an experience he refers to simply as “the war” before, with encouragement, giving a more concrete account.

He recalls an ambush in vivid fragments: the metallic crack of gunfire at close range, dirt striking his face as he dropped to the ground, the smell of fuel and burned earth, and the sight of another soldier collapsing beside him before Arun could make sense of what had happened. He remembers believing with complete certainty that he was about to die. What remains most striking in the way he tells it is how immediate it still feels to him. Even now, speaking in a therapist’s office decades later, he seems to brace in his chair at particular sensory details, as though his body is preparing for impact before his words catch up.

Since that time, his life has been marked by persistent posttraumatic symptoms that he has mostly tried to manage through endurance and silence. He reports recurrent, unwanted memories of combat that break into his day without warning, as well as distressing dreams that leave him waking abruptly and disoriented. At times he feels as if he is back there for an instant, especially when a loud bang or sudden mechanical noise catches him off guard. He describes becoming intensely upset around reminders of the war and notices strong physical reactions in those moments, with his heart pounding and his muscles tightening before he can settle himself.

The warehouse where he works has become one of the most difficult places for him, though it is also where he insists on proving he can still function. The slam of a loading dock door, the backfire of a truck in the yard, or the clatter of dropped metal can stop him cold. He does not talk about this with coworkers. Instead, he keeps to tasks at the edge of the floor when he can, avoids lingering near the loudest equipment, and times his breaks to spend as little time as possible in crowded common areas. Outside work, he has also shaped his life around not being reminded. He avoids war movies, avoids conversations about military service, and has gradually stopped attending community events where unexpected noise or commotion might unsettle him.

His daughter has noticed that this avoidance has not brought him peace so much as made his world smaller. Arun agrees with that description, though reluctantly. He says there are whole parts of his life he simply does not touch. He has little interest in socializing and describes feeling cut off from other people, including family. There is a flattening in the way he speaks about things he once cared about; very little feels genuinely enjoyable to him now. He also carries a steady watchfulness that he experiences as necessary rather than excessive. He scans rooms, notices exits immediately, and remains tense in public in a way that leaves him exhausted by the end of the day.

Sleep has become especially poor. He reports difficulty both falling and staying asleep, and he is often irritable from fatigue. He recognizes that he startles easily and can become sharp with coworkers when they approach him from behind or make sudden noise nearby. Although he is embarrassed by this, he also feels that people should know better than to come up on someone without warning. That conviction, like much else in his account, suggests how enduringly present danger still feels to him.

What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of strain. A recent incident at work, when a pallet dropped with a crash and he reacted so strongly that others stared, left him shaken and humiliated. His daughter later told him he seemed to be “living like the war never ended,” and for the first time he did not argue. Arun comes to treatment wary, proud, and tired. He says he does not expect to forget what happened and does not believe someone his age can become a different person. What he hopes, cautiously, is to sleep through the night and get through a workday without feeling ambushed by his own mind.
